rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Lengthen only the gradient to test whether the early critical pair responds to slope. The other pairs have ample resolution, so this comparison will indicate whether to refine gradient steepness or focus on temperature selectivity.

The critical pair improved only modestly with a shallower gradient, so test temperature selectivity at the original slope. Raising temperature may separate that pair while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Slightly flatten the gradient at the temperature that improved the critical pair. This should raise its resolution above 1.5 while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes, potentially reaching the maximum CRF of 1.0.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; now test a slightly steeper gradient to shorten the separation while retaining full resolution. This slope lies between injections 3 and 4, and the final organic fraction remains comfortably above the last peak’s estimated elution fraction.

Trim the gradient window to reduce separation time, keeping the starting fraction below the first peak’s estimated elution fraction and the endpoint above the last’s. The slope matches fully resolved injection 4, providing a useful test of whether the higher starting fraction preserves critical-pair selectivity.

Restore the lower starting fraction that favored the critical pair, and use a slope only slightly steeper than fully resolved injection 5. This should shorten the separation modestly while keeping all peaks within the gradient and targeting resolution just above 1.5.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 7 to approach the critical pair’s resolution limit while shortening the programmed gradient. The last peak may elute briefly into the final hold, so this run will check whether the lower endpoint offsets the time savings.

With CRF 1.0 secured, probe the opposite temperature extreme for an alternative selectivity window. The early pair may reverse order and separate more strongly at low temperature, potentially allowing a steeper, faster gradient in subsequent runs.

Move away from the late-peak coelution at 25 C while retaining some of the improved early-pair selectivity. A shorter gradient tests whether this lower-temperature window can support a faster fully resolved separation.

Test whether a substantially steeper gradient breaks up the late three-peak cluster at 25 C through slope-dependent selectivity. The early pair had excess resolution at this temperature, which may permit a shorter separation.

Return to the successful high-temperature region and flatten injection 6’s gradient by lowering the endpoint one step. This should recover full resolution of the early pair and test an alternative trimmed window, while keeping the last peak well below 10 minutes.

Explore a shifted starting window at an intermediate temperature, seeking a faster alternative to the established CRF-1.0 methods. The higher starting fraction tests early-pair selectivity, while 35 C may separate the late cluster better than 25–30 C.

Flatten the gradient and lower the starting fraction relative to injection 13 to improve both unresolved pairs. This tests whether the intermediate-temperature selectivity window can deliver full resolution in roughly seven minutes.

Test a small slope increase beyond injection 8, with a high endpoint that avoids its final-hold slowdown. This probes the fastest fully resolved boundary; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed CRF-1.0 method if the critical pair drops below 1.5.

Test a slope between injections 6 and 12 at the higher starting fraction, aiming to retain full resolution while shortening injection 12’s separation. The high endpoint keeps the last peak inside the gradient and isolates the slope adjustment.

Test whether further trimming the starting window can offset a shallower gradient and produce a faster fully resolved separation. The reduced slope is intended to compensate for the loss of early-pair resolution seen when the starting fraction increased.

With maximum CRF secured, test a more robust fully resolved method rather than further raising the starting fraction. This shallower gradient should improve the early critical pair while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes; monitor the middle pair, whose resolution decreases as the gradient flattens.

Increase the endpoint one step from injection 18 to shorten the separation while retaining a useful resolution margin. The slightly steeper slope should improve the middle critical pair and leave the early pair comfortably above 1.5.

Steepen injection 19 by one endpoint step to shorten the separation while preserving full resolution. Results at neighboring slopes suggest the critical early pair should retain a resolution margin above 1.5.

Shorten injection 20’s separation by raising the endpoint one step. This preserves the fully resolved slope of injection 4 in a shorter programmed gradient, targeting CRF 1.0 with more resolution margin than the fastest confirmed method.

Refine injection 16 with a slightly shallower slope to provide a small margin above its borderline early-pair resolution. The lower endpoint shortens the programmed gradient while remaining above the last peak’s elution window, targeting another CRF-1.0 method.

Test a nearby lower-temperature alternative with a shallower gradient to compensate for reduced early-pair selectivity. This may preserve CRF 1.0 below 10 minutes while improving the middle pair’s resolution relative to the shallow gradients at 60 C.

Restore 60 C while retaining injection 23’s trimmed gradient to recover early-pair resolution and shorten retention. Neighboring successful slopes suggest full resolution with a useful margin, provided the final hold keeps the last peak below 10 minutes.

Raise injection 24’s endpoint one step to shorten the separation while retaining a substantial resolution margin, targeting CRF 1.0. Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method; this final run tests a less borderline alternative.
